shortAnswer: A blurry KDP cover is almost always caused by low-resolution source images (below 300 DPI at print size), exporting as standard PDF instead of PDF Print, or JPEG compression applied during export. Replace low-quality images, verify your document DPI is 300, and re-export using PDF Print before uploading again.

faqs.question: Why does my KDP cover look blurry after upload?
faqs.answer: A blurry KDP cover is almost always caused by low-resolution source images below 300 DPI at print size, aggressive PDF compression during export, or using the wrong export format such as JPG or standard PDF instead of PDF Print. The cover may look fine on screen because monitors display at 72–96 DPI, while printing requires 300 DPI of actual pixel data.

faqs.question: Does Amazon KDP compress cover files after upload?
faqs.answer: KDP may apply processing to uploaded cover files, but the most common cause of blurry covers is compression that happens during export from your design tool before the file reaches KDP. Using PDF Print export settings in Canva or a high-quality PDF preset in Photoshop prevents most export compression problems.

faqs.question: Is 300 DPI required for KDP covers?
faqs.answer: Amazon KDP recommends 300 DPI for all cover images. Below 300 DPI, text and image detail can appear soft or blurry in print. This applies to the effective DPI at the final print size, not just the DPI setting in the document properties. A 300 DPI document setting does not help if the embedded images are originally low resolution.

faqs.question: Can Canva exports become blurry?
faqs.answer: Yes. The most common cause is downloading a standard PDF instead of PDF Print. In Canva, always select PDF as the file type and then choose Print quality rather than Standard. Also avoid using low-resolution imported images, screenshots, or small elements stretched to fill large areas of the cover.

faqs.question: Why does my text look fuzzy in KDP Previewer?
faqs.answer: Fuzzy text in KDP Previewer is usually caused by rasterized text that was converted from vector to pixels at insufficient resolution, compressed PDF export settings, or screenshots used as typography. Keep title and subtitle text as live vector layers and use PDF Print export to preserve sharp text outlines.

faqs.question: Can low-resolution AI images cause print problems?
faqs.answer: Yes. AI image generators often produce images at small default pixel dimensions such as 512×512 or 1024×1024 pixels. At full paperback cover size, those dimensions can drop below 300 effective DPI and produce blurry print results. Use AI generators that support high-resolution output, or run a quality upscaler before placing the image in your cover.

faqs.question: Should I use JPG or PDF for KDP covers?
faqs.answer: Use PDF Print for KDP paperback covers. JPEG export compresses images and can introduce compression artifacts, especially on dark backgrounds or detailed areas. PDF Print preserves the highest available image quality and is the format Amazon KDP recommends for print covers.

faqs.question: Why does my cover look fine on screen but blurry when printed?
faqs.answer: Screens display content at 72–96 DPI, which means low-resolution images look acceptable at screen viewing size. Printing requires 300 DPI. A 72 DPI image that looks sharp on a screen becomes visibly blurry when stretched to fill a physical print area that needs four times more pixel data per inch.

faqs.question: Can stretched images cause KDP rejection?
faqs.answer: KDP may warn about or reject covers with very low-resolution images. Even if a stretched image passes the upload check, it will likely print blurry or pixelated on paper. Always verify that every image is at least 300 DPI at the size it occupies in the final print layout before exporting.

faqs.question: How do I know if my cover is print quality?
faqs.answer: Check the effective DPI of every image at its final print size. Open the exported PDF and zoom in to 200–300% to look for soft or pixelated areas. Export using PDF Print rather than standard PDF or JPG. Use a preflight tool like KDPPreflight to scan for low-resolution assets and export problems before uploading to Amazon.

content:
If your KDP cover looked perfectly sharp before upload but suddenly appears blurry or pixelated inside Amazon KDP Previewer, the problem is almost never a KDP glitch. It is almost always caused by low-resolution source images, incorrect export settings, or compression applied somewhere in your design workflow.

A blurry KDP cover is one of the most frustrating quality problems self-published authors encounter, precisely because the file often looks fine on screen. Understanding why it happens is the first step to fixing it permanently.

This guide explains every major cause of a blurry kdp cover or pixelated kdp cover, how to diagnose which problem you have, and how to produce a sharp, print-ready result before reuploading.

## Why Your Cover Looks Sharp Locally but Blurry on KDP

Your design software and local PDF viewer are not showing you what the printer sees.

When you view a file in Canva, Photoshop, or Affinity, your screen automatically upscales or smooths low-resolution images to make them look acceptable at screen size. Screens display content at around 72 to 96 dots per inch. At that density, even a genuinely low-quality image can appear sharp. But printing works differently.

A physical print head deposits ink at 300 dots per inch or higher. If the image only contains 72 pixels of data per inch, the printer has to interpolate what the missing detail should look like. That interpolation produces blurry, soft, or pixelated print results.

KDP Previewer can reveal this problem even when the cover passes upload successfully. The Previewer applies a more production-accurate view than most local PDF viewers, which is why the low-quality KDP preview often surprises authors who felt confident about the design.

Zooming out also masks quality problems. A low-resolution image viewed at 10 or 20 percent of actual size can look perfectly fine. At 100 percent zoom in Photoshop, or at the resolution KDP applies during Previewer rendering, the same image shows soft edges, fuzzy details, and visible pixel squares.

There is one more hidden trap: PDF compression during export. Some design tools compress embedded images when creating a PDF. A design that contained a 300 DPI image may export with a compressed 72 DPI version embedded inside the PDF file. The artwork looked fine in the editor, but the exported PDF is using the lower-quality compressed version.

The principle to remember: a design that looks sharp on screen can still print poorly. Screen resolution and print resolution are not the same measurement.

## The Most Common Cause: Low DPI Images

DPI stands for dots per inch. It describes how many pixels of image information exist within one inch of the printed page.

At 72 DPI, a one-inch area of printed space contains only 72 pixels of image data. At 300 DPI, the same area contains 300 pixels. That difference is dramatic on paper and almost invisible on a screen.

Amazon KDP recommends 300 DPI for cover images. When a cover image is only 72 DPI and the design stretches it to paperback size, the printer must distribute those 72 pixels across what should be 300 pixels of physical space. The result is visible blur, soft edges, and in severe cases, obvious pixelation where individual colored squares become clearly visible.

A concrete example: a web-sized stock photo downloaded at 800 by 600 pixels is designed for screen viewing. On a 6-by-9 inch paperback front panel at 300 DPI, you need at least 1800 by 2700 pixels just for the front panel. That 800 by 600 image would be stretched to roughly 170 percent of its native size, producing an effective DPI of around 130. The result is a cover that looks fine in Canva but prints soft and blurry.

Stretching a low-resolution image does not add resolution. It only spreads the existing pixels further apart, making the problem worse, not better.

Low-DPI images are especially common when authors import stock photos from free websites, use screenshots of text or graphics, drag small AI-generated images into the design, or download images from social media platforms that compress uploads automatically.

## What Resolution Does Amazon KDP Require?

Amazon KDP recommends that cover images be at least 300 DPI at their final print size. This is not a vague guideline — it is the technical threshold below which print quality problems become visible under normal printing conditions.

For a standard 6 by 9 inch paperback front cover at 300 DPI, the front panel alone needs to be at least 1800 by 2700 pixels. A full wraparound cover with bleed and spine would require significantly more total pixels.

The pixel count matters more than the file size. A 15 MB image is not automatically high resolution. A 1 MB image is not automatically low resolution. The DPI relationship must be calculated by dividing the pixel dimensions by the physical print dimensions.

There is also an important difference between raster and vector graphics.

Raster images are made of pixels. JPG, PNG, and TIFF are raster formats. Their print quality is limited by the number of pixels they contain. Scale them too large and quality drops.

Vector graphics are made of mathematical paths and curves. Illustrator AI, SVG, and EPS files can contain vector artwork. Vectors can scale to any print size without losing quality because they are redrawn at the required resolution during export.

The best KDP cover workflow combines high-resolution raster photos or illustrations with vector text and vector decorative elements. This gives you the highest print quality across every element on the cover.

## Why Canva Covers Often Become Blurry

Canva is the most widely used design tool for self-publishers, and it is also the source of many blurry KDP covers. Understanding the specific Canva pitfalls helps you avoid them permanently.

**Importing low-quality images from external sources.** Many authors find images on free sites, download them, and drag them into Canva. If the source image is 72 DPI or web-optimized, that quality problem is imported directly into the design. Canva cannot add pixel data that was never in the original file.

**Using screenshots as cover elements.** Screenshots are screen-resolution images, typically 72 to 144 DPI even on high-density Retina screens. A screenshot of a graphic, logo, or text element will almost always be too low resolution for print at full cover size.

**Stretching small elements to fill large areas.** A Canva element that looks fine at thumbnail size may be a small image stretched to fill a large portion of the cover. Stretching does not increase pixel count. It increases visible pixelation.

**Compressed image uploads.** When images are uploaded to Canva, the platform may apply its own compression depending on the source file quality and account type. The image you placed may already be lower resolution than the file you uploaded.

**Downloading as standard PDF instead of PDF Print.** This is the single most common Canva mistake. When a Canva user selects Share, then Download, then PDF, they may receive a standard PDF with compressed images. PDF Print is a separate option that requires selecting PDF from the file type list and then choosing Print quality rather than Standard quality. Always verify which type you are downloading.

**Low-quality marketplace elements.** Third-party elements available in the Canva marketplace may include low-resolution artwork designed for screen presentation. Elements that look great at card size can be inadequate for a full-bleed cover background at print resolution.

Before uploading your Canva cover to KDP, run it through [KDPPreflight](/tools/kdp-cover-checker) to detect image quality issues, low-resolution assets, and export problems before Amazon flags them.

## Photoshop, Affinity, and Illustrator Quality Problems

Professional design tools give you full control, which also means more ways to introduce quality problems if the settings are incorrect.

**Incorrect document DPI.** In Photoshop or Affinity Photo, the document resolution is set when the file is created. If the document was started at 72 DPI, every layer and element inherits that resolution. Changing DPI later through Image Size may resample the document incorrectly and produce blurry results. Always create print cover documents at 300 DPI from the beginning.

**Wrong PDF export preset.** Photoshop and Affinity offer multiple PDF export presets including smallest file, standard, and high quality print. Choosing the wrong preset can compress embedded images aggressively. Always use a high-quality print or press-quality PDF preset for KDP covers.

**Rasterized text layers.** In Photoshop, text layers can accidentally be rasterized during editing or flattening. Once rasterized, text becomes a pixel image. If rasterized at insufficient resolution, text will appear blurry in print. Keep text as live vector layers whenever possible.

**Embedded low-resolution images.** Even inside a 300 DPI Photoshop document, individual placed images may be lower resolution. A placed image that is natively 72 DPI remains 72 DPI inside the document regardless of the document-level DPI setting. Check each image individually.

**Aggressive JPEG compression in PDF export.** If the export dialog compresses embedded JPEGs too strongly, images inside the final PDF will be lower quality than the originals in the source file. Check the compression slider in the PDF export settings and set it to maximum quality or lossless.

**Scaling artwork after export.** If the exported PDF is processed by another tool, converted, or scaled before upload, the effective resolution can decrease. Upload the original exported PDF directly to KDP without intermediate processing.

## How to Check If an Image Is Too Low Resolution

Before exporting the final cover, take a few minutes to verify every image in the design meets print quality standards.

**Calculate effective DPI by dividing pixel width by print width.** If an image is 800 pixels wide and occupies 4 inches of the cover, that is 800 divided by 4, which equals 200 DPI. Too low for print. Repeat this for every raster image in the design.

**Zoom to 100 percent in your design tool.** At 100 percent view in Photoshop or Affinity, you are seeing the design close to its actual print-scale relationship. If images look soft or pixelated at 100 percent, they will likely print that way.

**Look for soft edges.** Sharp print images have crisp, clean boundaries between elements, text, and shapes. If you see feathered or blurred edges where there should be hard contrast, the image is probably below print resolution.

**Open the exported PDF and zoom in.** Open the cover PDF in Acrobat or another PDF viewer that supports high-zoom inspection. Zoom to 200 or 300 percent on important image and text areas. If the content looks pixelated at high zoom, the embedded image resolution is likely insufficient.

**Check individual image properties.** In Photoshop, select a placed image and use Image > Image Size to see the actual pixel dimensions and current resolution. Compare those numbers against the physical print dimensions the image occupies.

## Why Text Sometimes Looks Blurry on KDP

Text on KDP covers looks blurry for a small number of specific reasons.

**Rasterized text.** When text is converted from a live vector format to pixels during editing or export, it becomes raster text. If that rasterization happens at low resolution, the text edges become soft. In Photoshop, avoid rasterizing text layers during editing. Export with settings that preserve live text or convert text to vector outlines rather than pixels.

**Text converted to pixels during export.** Some export workflows convert live text to raster images inside the PDF rather than embedding it as vector paths or font data. A high-quality print PDF preset should prevent this. Verify by zooming in to the exported PDF. Vector text stays sharp at any zoom level. Raster text becomes obviously pixelated when zoomed in.

**Screenshots used as typography.** If the original font file is unavailable and you capture the text as a screenshot to use it as an image element, the screenshot will be raster typography at screen resolution. It will always look softer than real vector text at print scale.

**Aggressive PDF compression applied to fonts.** Some PDF export tools or compression passes can affect how embedded font data renders, particularly in very aggressively compressed output files. Use a high-quality export preset to prevent this.

Vector text consistently prints sharper than raster text. This is especially important for title typography, author names, and subtitle text where any softness is immediately visible.

## Full-Black Covers and Compression Problems

Solid-black and dark-background covers are popular for coloring books, puzzle books, journals, and notebooks. These covers are particularly vulnerable to revealing compression artifacts that lighter covers hide.

Compression works by simplifying areas of similar color. In a bright, colorful image, small compression artifacts are often invisible at normal viewing distance. On a solid dark background, even very small differences in color value become visible as faint blocks, banding patterns, or patches of slightly different darkness.

This is a real problem for coloring book covers and dark paperbacks. An area that should be perfectly smooth black may show subtle compression blocks that print as visible squares or bands of slightly different tone. The cover looks fine on screen but appears streaked or blotchy in print.

JPEG compression is the primary culprit. JPEG is a lossy format that always introduces compression artifacts, particularly in flat color areas and smooth gradients. A solid black background saved or exported as JPEG will often contain faint blocky artifacts invisible on screen but visible in print.

Gradients on dark covers are especially risky. A gradient from black to dark charcoal that looks smooth on a monitor may band or show visible tonal steps when printed because compression reduces the number of distinct color values in the gradient.

The fix for dark covers is to use PDF Print export rather than JPG, keep backgrounds as solid flat color fills rather than JPEG-compressed images, and avoid placing dark paper texture images that were saved as JPEG in the design. Use PNG or vector-based backgrounds for dark-cover designs where compression artifacts are most visible.

## Common Image Mistakes That Cause Blurry Covers

**Screenshots used as artwork.** Any screenshot is screen resolution and will almost always be too low quality for print at full cover size. Do not use screenshots of text, graphics, icons, or other visual elements as cover artwork.

**AI images exported too small.** AI image generators often default to 512 by 512 or 1024 by 1024 pixel output. At 6-by-9 inch paperback print size, a 1024 pixel image produces roughly 170 effective DPI. Use AI generators that support high-resolution output, or use a quality upscaler specifically designed for print resolution before placing the image in your cover design.

**Stretched PNGs.** A 400 pixel wide PNG element stretched to fill 4 inches of the cover is only 100 effective DPI at that position. Always check the pixel dimensions versus the physical size in the design before exporting.

**Images downloaded from social media.** Social platforms compress uploaded images heavily. A photo posted to Instagram or Facebook and then redownloaded is a compressed, degraded version of the original. Never use social media as a source for cover artwork.

**Exporting as JPG instead of PDF Print.** JPG export applies lossy compression to the entire cover. PDF Print preserves the highest quality available from the source files. For KDP covers, PDF Print is always the correct export choice.

**Upscaling tiny graphics without verifying quality.** Using an AI upscaler or Photoshop resample to enlarge a small image can improve quality, but it cannot fully restore detail that was never captured in the original file. Always verify that upscaled images still look sharp at 100 percent zoom and at 300 percent zoom in the exported PDF.

## How to Fix a Blurry KDP Cover

### Step 1: Check Source Image Resolution

Review every image in the cover design. Calculate the effective DPI at the size each image occupies by dividing pixel width by physical print width in inches. Flag any image below 300 effective DPI.

### Step 2: Verify Document DPI

In Photoshop or Affinity, confirm the document resolution is 300 DPI. In Canva, the effective DPI is determined by the design dimensions and the pixel size of placed images. There is no global DPI setting in Canva, so you must check each image individually.

### Step 3: Replace Low-Quality Assets

Any image below 300 DPI at print size must be replaced with a higher-resolution version. Find the original source file if available. If not, source a print-quality replacement from a stock image platform that provides high-resolution downloads, or use an AI upscaler to increase the resolution of existing assets before placing them.

### Step 4: Export as PDF Print

In Canva: Share > Download > File Type: PDF > Quality: Print. In Photoshop: File > Export or Save As PDF with a high quality print preset. In Affinity Publisher: File > Export > PDF with the For Print preset. Do not use standard PDF, JPG, or PNG for KDP cover uploads.

### Step 5: Avoid Unnecessary Compression

Do not open the exported PDF and re-save it in another application without checking compression settings. Do not send the file through messaging apps or email attachments that may compress it. Do not convert PDF to JPG and re-upload. Upload the original exported PDF file directly.

### Step 6: Keep Text Vector-Based

Use PDF export settings that preserve text as embedded font data or outlined vector paths, not converted to raster images. This keeps all text elements perfectly sharp at any print scale regardless of the document DPI.

### Step 7: Inspect the Final PDF at Zoom

Open the exported PDF in Acrobat or a comparable PDF viewer. Zoom in to 200 to 300 percent on text-heavy areas and image areas. If the cover looks sharp at high zoom, it should print well. If you see pixelation or soft edges, return to Steps 1 through 3.

### Step 8: Upload to KDP Previewer Again

Upload the corrected cover to KDP and inspect the Previewer carefully. Check all text elements, image-heavy areas, edges, and dark background sections. If the Previewer still looks blurry, repeat the resolution check and export process.

Before reuploading, run your corrected file through [KDPPreflight](/tools/kdp-cover-checker) to confirm resolution, image quality, bleed, and export settings are all correct before sending the file to Amazon.

## Best Export Settings for Sharp KDP Covers

### Canva Export Settings

Select PDF as the file type, then choose Print quality rather than Standard. If your design extends to the cover edge, ensure the bleed option is enabled. Do not add crop marks unless you specifically need them and understand how they change PDF dimensions. Download from a browser, not the Canva mobile app, and upload the same file without re-compressing or converting it.

### Photoshop Export Settings

Create the document at 300 DPI before designing. Export as PDF using a High Quality Print or PDF/X-1a preset. Set image compression to ZIP or minimal JPEG compression at quality 10 or higher. Use sRGB color mode for best KDP compatibility. Flatten the document at full document resolution before export, and verify the exported PDF page dimensions match your intended cover size.

### Affinity Publisher and Affinity Photo Settings

Export as PDF using the For Print or PDF/X-1b preset. Set image quality to Maximum. Rasterize any unsupported blending modes at 300 DPI or higher. Verify the exported PDF at zoom before uploading.

### Illustrator Settings

Use Save as PDF with a print-quality preset. Ensure all placed raster images are embedded at their original resolution. Keep title and subtitle typography as outlined vector paths. Confirm the artboard dimensions match the full cover size including bleed before exporting.

## How to Prevent Blurry Covers Before Uploading

**Start with large source assets.** Always use source images larger than you think you need. An image slightly too large can be scaled down cleanly. An image too small cannot be fixed without quality loss.

**Use print-quality image sources.** Source photos and illustrations from stock platforms that offer high-resolution downloads. Create original artwork at 300 DPI from the beginning. Use AI image generators that support high-resolution output.

**Avoid stretching raster images.** Once a raster image is placed in the design, do not scale it beyond its native resolution. Verify the effective DPI after any resize before proceeding to export.

**Inspect at 100 percent before exporting.** Zoom your design tool to 100 percent and look for any soft or blurry areas in images and text. What you see at 100 percent is a close approximation of the print-scale result.

**Export correctly the first time.** Choose PDF Print in Canva. Choose a high-quality or press-quality preset in Photoshop or Affinity. Do not export as JPG or as a standard PDF.

**Avoid repeated compression.** Each time an image is exported, edited, and re-exported, it can lose quality incrementally. Work from original high-resolution sources and export the final cover only once from the source file.

**Use a preflight checking tool.** A [KDP cover checker](/tools/kdp-cover-checker) can scan your exported PDF for resolution problems, low-quality images, and export issues before you upload. This is significantly faster than waiting for KDP to reject or Previewer to reveal problems after upload.

For understanding safe areas and bleed on your cover, see the [safe area glossary](/glossary/safe-area). For cover dimension issues that often accompany export problems, see the [KDP cover size mismatch guide](/blog/kdp-cover-size-does-not-match-interior) and the [cropped cover guide](/blog/kdp-cover-uploaded-successfully-but-looks-cropped).

## Quick Checklist Before Uploading Again

- All images are at least 300 DPI at their print size
- No images imported from screenshots, social media, or web searches
- No raster images stretched beyond native resolution
- Document DPI confirmed at 300 in Photoshop or Affinity
- Text kept as vector paths, not rasterized pixels
- Cover exported as PDF Print, not standard PDF or JPG
- Final exported PDF inspected at 200 percent zoom
- No dark-background JPEG compression artifacts visible
- Vectors preserved throughout the export process
- File uploaded is the latest corrected export

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why does my KDP cover look blurry after upload?

A blurry KDP cover is almost always caused by low-resolution source images below 300 DPI at print size, aggressive PDF compression during export, or using the wrong export format. The cover may look fine on screen because monitors show content at 72 to 96 DPI while printing requires 300 DPI of actual image data.

### Does Amazon KDP compress cover files after upload?

KDP processes uploaded cover files, but the most common cause of blurry covers is compression that happens during export from your design tool before the file reaches Amazon. Using PDF Print settings in Canva or a high-quality PDF preset in Photoshop solves most export compression problems.

### Is 300 DPI required for KDP covers?

Amazon KDP recommends 300 DPI for all cover images. Below 300 DPI, text and image detail can appear soft or blurry in print. This applies to the effective DPI of each image at its final print size, not just the DPI value in your document settings.

### Can Canva exports become blurry?

Yes. The most common cause is downloading standard PDF instead of PDF Print. In Canva, always select PDF as the file type and then choose Print quality. Also avoid using low-resolution imports, screenshots, or small elements that have been stretched to fill large cover areas.

### Why does my text look fuzzy in KDP Previewer?

Fuzzy text in KDP Previewer is usually caused by rasterized text converted from vector to pixels at low resolution, compressed PDF export settings, or screenshots used in place of real font files. Keep text as live vector layers and use PDF Print export to preserve sharp outlines.

### Can low-resolution AI images cause print problems?

Yes. AI image generators often output at small default dimensions like 512 by 512 or 1024 by 1024 pixels. At full paperback cover size those dimensions may produce below 300 effective DPI, resulting in blurry print quality. Always verify output pixel dimensions and use a quality upscaler if needed.

### Should I use JPG or PDF for KDP covers?

Use PDF Print for all KDP paperback cover uploads. JPEG compression introduces artifacts especially on dark backgrounds and detailed areas. PDF Print preserves the highest quality from your source files and is the format Amazon KDP recommends for print covers.

### Why does my cover look fine on screen but blurry when printed?

Screens display at 72 to 96 DPI, making low-resolution images look acceptable. Printing at 300 DPI requires four times more pixel data per inch than a typical screen provides. A 72 DPI image that looks sharp on screen appears visibly blurry when expanded to its physical print dimensions.

### Can stretched images cause KDP rejection?

KDP may warn about or reject covers with very low-resolution images. Even if a stretched image passes the upload check, it will print blurry or pixelated on paper. Always verify that every image reaches at least 300 effective DPI at its position in the final print layout.

### How do I know if my cover is print quality?

Calculate effective DPI for every image by dividing pixel width by the physical width in inches it occupies. Open the exported PDF and zoom to 200 or 300 percent looking for soft or pixelated areas. Export as PDF Print rather than standard PDF or JPG. Use a preflight tool to catch low-resolution assets before uploading.

## Final Check Before You Upload Again

A blurry KDP cover is almost always a technical problem you can fix before upload, not after rejection. With the right source images, a 300 DPI document, and a PDF Print export, most covers will pass KDP quality checks and look sharp in the Previewer.

Before uploading your paperback again, run your file through [KDPPreflight](/tools/kdp-cover-checker) to detect low-resolution assets, blurry images, unsafe exports, and print-quality problems before Amazon KDP catches them.
